about: Worked examples from the Social Security operating manual (POMS) and the SSI regulations (20 CFR Part 416) that Giftwise cites, each about a gift or similar help to one person. Every passage is SSA's own text. Dates are moved to 2026 so 2026 amounts apply; the facts are SSA's, and where SSA's example gives no amount, an amount is supplied that does not change SSA's answer. Expected answers are SSA's, except three food examples written before the 2024 rule that stopped counting food, which are marked. Examples Giftwise does not model are listed with the reason, not scored.

measures.after_infrequent: Income from the gift in that month after the $60 infrequent or irregular income exclusion, before the $20 general exclusion.
measures.ism_value: In-kind support (housing) charged for that month, before exclusions.
measures.ssi_amount: The SSI amount that month's income gives, before the two-month payment lag.

findings.found: The first run matched 11 of 13. SSA counts football tickets given as a gift as income at their value, but Giftwise had no category for tickets and treated every gift of an item as something for personal use.
findings.fixed: Giftwise now has an event tickets category, counted at its value whether the tickets are given or bought straight from the box office (rule R-ITEM-02).

findings.found: When a relative prepays a bill that covers future months, SSA charges in-kind support in each month the bill covers. Giftwise counted it only in the month it was paid, so it matched June but not July to December.
findings.fixed: A housing bill can now carry the months it covers. The share for months up to the payment counts when it is paid, and each later month's share counts in that month (rule R-SHEL-02). This example and a new one, next month's rent paid early, now match.

findings.found: Two of the new examples (POMS SI 00810.410 L.3) did not match. SSA applies the $60 one-off exclusion in the order income arrives, and to housing help at its actual value before the monthly cap. Giftwise applied it after the cap, so for a one-off housing payment above the cap it counted $60 less than SSA and showed a check $60 too high.
findings.fixed: Giftwise now applies the exclusion in order of receipt and before the cap (rule R-INFREQ-01). Both orders in SSA's example match, with a unit test for each.

cases.title: A sister pays the phone bill
cases.passage: Joshua Hall, an SSI recipient, is unable to pay his phone bill so his sister pays the phone company with her own money. Neither the payment to the phone company nor the telephone service received as a result of the payment is income because it is not food or shelter.
cases.situation: Joshua receives SSI and lives alone. In April 2026 he cannot pay his $85 phone bill, so his sister pays the phone company $85 from her own money.
cases.question: Does the $85 count as income to Joshua?
cases.ssa_answer: Not income: the payment is not for food or shelter.

cases.title: A daughter pays the grocer
cases.passage: The daughter of Mrs. Harper, an SSI recipient, pays the grocer for food delivered to her mother. Although the payment to the grocer is not income, Mrs. Harper receives ISM in the form of food, subject to the PMV (SI 00835.300).
cases.situation: Mrs. Harper receives SSI and lives alone in her own apartment. In April 2026 her daughter pays the grocer $250 for food delivered to her mother.
cases.question: Does the $250 count as income to Mrs. Harper?
cases.ssa_answer: When written (2005): in-kind support in the form of food. Since September 30, 2024: not income.

updated.note: SSA wrote this example in 2005, when food paid for by others counted as in-kind support. A 2024 rule removed food from in-kind support, so today it is not income.

cases.title: An adult child pays off a grocery tab
cases.passage: Situation - Shawn buys their food at a neighborhood store where they have a line of credit. In August 2011, Shawn purchased $150 worth of groceries and received the bill in September. Shawn asked their adult child for help in making the payment, and on September 28, without expectation of repayment, the adult child paid the grocer $100, leaving a $50 unpaid balance. b. Analysis - Although the food was available to Shawn in August, Shawn was under obligation to pay for it and it was not income. Some of the food became income to Shawn in September when the adult child made the $100 vendor payment. Since $100 is less than the PMV, we charge Shawn with $100 ISM in September. Shawn is still responsible for paying the $50 balance, so that amount was not income to Shawn.
cases.situation: Shawn receives SSI and lives alone. He bought $150 of groceries on credit at a neighborhood store. On September 28, 2026 his adult child pays the grocer $100 toward the bill, with no expectation of repayment, leaving $50 that Shawn still owes.
cases.question: Does the $100 count as income to Shawn in September 2026?
cases.ssa_answer: When written (2011): $100 of in-kind support. Since September 30, 2024: not income.

updated.note: SSA wrote this example for 2011, when food counted as in-kind support. Since September 30, 2024 it does not.

cases.title: A relative pays a whole year's property tax
cases.passage: Situation - Kelly, who lives alone, received an $800 tax bill on their home in June 2011. The bill covered the tax period from January through December of the same year. Kelly's relative paid the tax bill in full on June 30 (five months retrospectively, one month current, and six months prospectively). b. Analysis - Kelly received ISM valued at $400, subject to the PMV, in June because their relative paid the tax bill in that month, which covered the period January through June. Kelly also received monthly ISM valued at $66.66 from July through December, the period that a shelter item was prepaid.
cases.situation: Kelly receives SSI and lives alone in a home she owns. In June 2026 she receives an $800 property tax bill covering January through December 2026. On June 30, 2026 a relative pays the whole bill as a gift.
cases.question: How much in-kind support does Kelly receive in June, July and December 2026?
cases.ssa_answer: In-kind support of $400 in June (six months of the bill), capped at the 2026 limit of $351.33, then $66.67 in each month from July to December.
cases.input_note: The tax payment is entered with the months it covers, January to December 2026.

cases.title: A brother provides water and electricity
cases.passage: James Smith, an eligible individual, lives alone in a house trailer they own. The trailer is situated on the property of their sibling, Bill. James pays no rent for the use of the land. Bill provides water and electricity free of charge. The free use of the land results in no ISM to James. However, James is charged with outside ISM based on the CMV of the water and electricity.
cases.situation: James receives SSI and lives alone in a trailer he owns, on land his brother Bill owns. James pays no rent for the land. Every month Bill provides the water and electricity free of charge; in June 2026 they are worth $90.
cases.question: Does the free water and electricity count as income to James in June 2026, and how much?
cases.ssa_answer: In-kind support at the value of the water and electricity. The free use of the land is not.

cases.title: Someone outside pays the electric bill of a shared home
cases.passage: An eligible individual and their friend live in a house the friend owns. The friend buys all of the food for the household and pays all the shelter expenses except for electricity. The friend's parent pays the electric bill each month. Based on the eligible individual receiving both food and shelter from the household and not paying their pro rata share, the eligible individual is subject to the VTR. Because the VTR applies, no additional ISM will count. Therefore, the electric bill paid by someone outside the household will not count as ISM.
cases.situation: Rosa receives SSI and lives in a house her friend owns. The friend pays all the shelter costs except electricity, and Rosa does not pay her share. Each month the friend's parent, who lives elsewhere, pays the $100 electric bill. Consider June 2026.
cases.question: Does the parent paying the $100 electric bill add any income for Rosa in June 2026?
cases.ssa_answer: No. The one-third reduction already applies because she lives in another person's household, so the electric bill adds no in-kind support.

cases.title: Birthday cash, then a small lottery win
cases.passage: Situation: A recipient receives a birthday gift of $100 cash in January and wins $25 in March playing the State lottery. Analysis: Since the income received is no more than once a quarter, its receipt is infrequent. Since neither could be anticipated, both are also irregular. The $60 infrequent or irregular income exclusion reduces the $100 to $40 since it is the first infrequent or irregular income received in that quarter. The $25 received in March is not affected by the infrequent or irregular income exclusion.
cases.situation: Ana receives SSI and lives alone with no other income. On January 15, 2026 she receives a $100 birthday gift in cash. On March 20, 2026 she wins $25 in the state lottery.
cases.question: How much of each counts as income, after the infrequent or irregular income exclusion?
cases.ssa_answer: The $60 quarterly exclusion takes the $100 down to $40. The $25 in March is not reduced, because that quarter's $60 is used up.

cases.title: Loan interest, then football tickets from the same friend
cases.passage: Evaluating each receipt separately, we see that each can qualify separately as infrequent. The first $60 is excludable even though the total received exceeds $60. The infrequent or irregular income exclusion would reduce the $50 interest income in July to zero and the remaining $10 exclusion would reduce the value of the tickets to $90.
cases.situation: Ben receives SSI and lives alone with no other income. In July 2026 a friend repays a loan with $50 of interest. In August 2026 the same friend gives Ben football tickets worth $100.
cases.question: How much of the interest and of the tickets counts as income, after the infrequent or irregular income exclusion?
cases.ssa_answer: Each type of income is judged on its own. The $60 exclusion takes the interest to $0 and the tickets to $90.
cases.input_note: Interest is not a gift, so it is entered as income from a separate source, which is how SSA evaluates two types of income from one person.

cases.title: A gift of jewelry she wears
cases.passage: If a gift of jewelry retained into the month after the month of receipt is excluded from resources as part of an individual's personal effects, it does not count as income. For more information on the personal effects exclusion, see SI 01130.430. If the jewelry is not an excluded resource, it is counted as unearned income at its CMV.
cases.situation: Lena receives SSI and lives alone. In February 2026 her mother gives her a $300 necklace, which Lena wears every day and keeps.
cases.question: Does the necklace count as income to Lena?
cases.ssa_answer: Not income, because jewelry she wears is an excluded personal effect.

cases.title: A gift of a car, her only one
cases.passage: A gift of a car that qualifies as a wholly or partially excluded resource if retained into the month after the month of receipt is not income. If the car does not qualify as a wholly or partially excluded resource (e.g., it is a second car), the car is counted as income in the month it is received.
cases.situation: Omar receives SSI and lives alone. He does not own a car. In May 2026 his uncle gives him a car worth $8,000, which Omar uses to get to work and appointments.
cases.question: Does the car count as income to Omar?
cases.ssa_answer: Not income, because one car is an excluded resource.

cases.title: A cash gift
cases.passage: A gift of cash is counted as unearned income. For benefits payable on or after June 1, 2004, a gift used for paying tuition, fees, or other necessary educational expenses at an educational institution is excluded from income in the month received and from resources for nine months beginning the month after the month of receipt. For benefits payable on or after July 1, 2004, the first $60 received from gifts of cash in a calendar quarter might be excludable as infrequent or irregular income.
cases.situation: Grace receives SSI and lives alone with no other income. In May 2026 her cousin gives her $200 in cash. It is the only gift she receives that quarter.
cases.question: How much of the $200 counts as income, after the infrequent or irregular income exclusion?
cases.ssa_answer: Cash is unearned income. The first $60 in a quarter can be excluded as infrequent, leaving $140.

cases.title: A cash gift used for tuition
cases.passage: A gift of cash is counted as unearned income. For benefits payable on or after June 1, 2004, a gift used for paying tuition, fees, or other necessary educational expenses at an educational institution is excluded from income in the month received and from resources for nine months beginning the month after the month of receipt. For benefits payable on or after July 1, 2004, the first $60 received from gifts of cash in a calendar quarter might be excludable as infrequent or irregular income.
cases.situation: Theo receives SSI and lives alone. In August 2026 his grandparents give him $1,500 in cash, which he uses that month to pay tuition and fees at his community college.
cases.question: Does the $1,500 count as income to Theo?
cases.ssa_answer: Not income: a gift used for tuition, fees or other necessary educational expenses is excluded.

cases.title: A scholarship and a grant used for school
cases.passage: An SSI beneficiary who attends an educational institution receives a $1,000 scholarship and a $1,000 grant in September 2004. The educational assistance is not under Title IV of HEA or BIA. The student uses $1,500 to pay for tuition, fees, and other necessary educational expenses in September 2004. The student plans to use the remaining $500 to help pay tuition, fees, and other educational expenses in February 2005. The claims representative verifies the type and amount of assistance and expenses and excludes $2,000 from income in September 2004 because this assistance is or will be used to pay tuition, fees or other necessary educational expenses.
cases.situation: Mia receives SSI, lives alone and attends college. In September 2026 she receives a $1,000 scholarship and a $1,000 grant, neither under the Higher Education Act. She uses $1,500 for tuition and fees that month and keeps $500 for next term's tuition.
cases.question: How much of the $2,000 counts as income to Mia in September 2026?
cases.ssa_answer: None. All $2,000 is excluded because it is, or will be, used for tuition, fees or other necessary educational expenses.

cases.title: A sister pays the mortgage, then a friend gives birthday cash
cases.passage: Situation: A claimant files for SSI in September 2023. In that month, the claimant receives a birthday gift of $25 cash from a friend on September 15. Also on September 2, the claimant's sister, who lives elsewhere, pays the claimant's $500 mortgage payment directly to the mortgage company “just to help my sibling out this month.” Analysis: Both sources of income are infrequent and irregular. However, since the $500 payment was received first, the $60 exclusion reduces the amount to $440. This $440 is subject to the $324.66 PMV (2023 rate), so in September, we count ISM of $324.66 and cash of $25.
cases.situation: Dana receives SSI and lives alone in a home she owns, with no other income. On September 2, 2026 her sister, who lives elsewhere, pays Dana's $500 mortgage payment directly to the mortgage company, just to help that month. On September 15, 2026 a friend gives Dana $25 in cash for her birthday.
cases.question: In September 2026, how much in-kind support is charged, and how much of the mortgage payment and the cash counts after the infrequent or irregular income exclusion?
cases.ssa_answer: The $500 came first, so the $60 exclusion takes it to $440, which is still over the cap. The cap is charged ($324.66 in 2023, $351.33 in 2026) and the $25 cash counts in full.

cases.title: The same two gifts, with the cash first
cases.passage: NOTE: If the cash birthday gift had been received first, the $25 would have been excluded as infrequent or irregular income and the $500 mortgage payment would have been reduced to $465 by the remaining $35 of the infrequent or irregular income exclusion. The $465 remaining mortgage payment would then be subject to the $324.66 PMV.
cases.situation: Dana receives SSI and lives alone in a home she owns, with no other income. On September 2, 2026 a friend gives Dana $25 in cash for her birthday. On September 15, 2026 her sister, who lives elsewhere, pays Dana's $500 mortgage payment directly to the mortgage company.
cases.question: In September 2026, how much of the cash and the mortgage payment counts after the infrequent or irregular income exclusion?
cases.ssa_answer: The $25 cash came first and is excluded. The other $35 of the exclusion takes the $500 to $465, still over the cap, so the cap is charged ($351.33 in 2026).

cases.title: A bank's one-time adjustment on top of regular interest
cases.passage: An individual has a savings account that pays interest of $15 in the second month of each quarter. The interest has been routinely excluded as infrequent as the individual has no other infrequent or irregular income. In 2023, without any advance notice to depositors, the bank changes its accounting system. As a result, in June the individual receives a $2.03 one-time payment in addition to their regular $15 interest payment in May. The bank does not intend to interrupt its usual quarterly interest schedule, so the CR correctly views the one-time payment in June as being from a separate source than the regular quarterly payments; i.e., it is a bank adjustment. Therefore, the regular $15 payment is still excludable as infrequent while the unexpected $2.03 payment is irregular. The total is within the $20 limit in the month of receipt and is excludable.
cases.situation: Ruth receives SSI and lives alone with no other income. Her savings account pays $15 interest in the second month of each quarter. In May 2026 she gets her regular $15. In June 2026, after the bank changes its accounting system without notice, it also pays her a one-time $2.03 adjustment.
cases.question: How much of the May interest and the June adjustment counts as income, after the infrequent or irregular income exclusion?
cases.ssa_answer: Neither counts. The quarterly interest is infrequent and the unexpected adjustment is irregular, and both fit within the exclusion.
cases.input_note: Interest is not a gift, so each payment is entered as income from its own source, which is how SSA evaluates them.

cases.title: A daughter buys a furnace on the utility bill
cases.passage: William's adult child Amber purchased a furnace for William's home when the old furnace stopped working. Amber bought the furnace from the local utility company and paid for it in monthly installments on a utility bill. The utility company confirmed that William cannot return the furnace for cash since Amber made the purchase and it was purchased on credit. Therefore, the gift of the furnace is not income to William.
cases.situation: William receives SSI and lives alone in his own home. In January 2026 his furnace stops working, and his adult daughter Amber buys him a new $3,600 furnace from the local utility company, paying for it in monthly installments on a utility bill. William cannot return the furnace for cash.
cases.question: Does the furnace count as income to William?
cases.ssa_answer: Not income. The furnace was bought on credit and cannot be returned for cash.

cases.title: A brother buys a mobile home and pays the loan
cases.passage: Victoria is an aged beneficiary living in an apartment. The landlord raises the rent. Victoria's sibling, Alfred, decides to buy Victoria a mobile home to live in so that Victoria can move from the apartment. Alfred puts the mobile home in both their names. Alfred makes a down payment of $4,000 in April 2011, and loan payments of $400 each month thereafter. Victoria moves into the mobile home in April, and lives there alone. The sibling's down payment of $4,000 in April is ISM to Victoria. Alfred's loan payment of $400 beginning in May is a shelter payment and is outside ISM. Since the actual value of each source of ISM exceeds the PMV, we charge the PMV for April 2011 and continuing. For more information on ISM to one person, see SI 00835.400A. For more information on ISM from outside household, see SI 00835.350.
cases.situation: Victoria receives SSI and lives alone with no other income. Her brother Alfred buys a mobile home for her, in both their names. He makes a $4,000 down payment in April 2026, and she moves in that month. From May 2026 he makes the $400 loan payment each month.
cases.question: How much in-kind support is charged in April and in May 2026?
cases.ssa_answer: Both the down payment and the loan payments are in-kind support for shelter. Each is over the cap, so the cap is charged ($351.33 in 2026) in April and every month after.
cases.input_note: The down payment and the loan payments are both entered as payments for her home, since payments on a mobile home count as mortgage payments (POMS SI 00835.465D.2).

cases.title: A daughter pays the mortgage every month
cases.passage: Examples: If your daughter uses her own money to pay your mortgage payment directly to the mortgage lender, the payment itself is not your income because you do not receive it. However, because of your daughter's payment, the transaction provides you with shelter; the mortgage payment is in-kind income for shelter to you.
cases.situation: Helen receives SSI and lives alone in a house she owns, with no other income. Every month in 2026 her daughter uses her own money to pay Helen's $620 mortgage payment directly to the lender. Consider March 2026.
cases.question: How much in-kind support is charged in March 2026, and what is Helen's SSI amount for that month?
cases.ssa_answer: The payment itself is not income, but the shelter it provides is in-kind income. Under the presumed value rule it is capped at $351.33 in 2026, so after the $20 general exclusion her SSI is $662.67.

cases.title: A son pays a hotel bill the month after the stay
cases.passage: Similarly, if you book a hotel room on credit and your son later pays the bill, the payment to the hotel is not income to you, but the payment of the bill is in-kind income for shelter to you. In this example, if your son pays for the hotel bill in a month after the month of the hotel stay, we will count the in-kind income to you in the month in which he pays the bill.
cases.situation: Grace receives SSI and lives alone with no other income. In March 2026 she books a hotel room on credit for three nights, costing $240. In April 2026 her son pays the hotel bill.
cases.question: In which month is in-kind support charged, and how much, for March and April 2026?
cases.ssa_answer: In-kind income for shelter of $240, counted in April, the month her son pays, not in March.

cases.title: A brother pays for lawn mowing
cases.passage: On the other hand, if your brother pays a lawn service to mow your grass, the payment is not income to you because the mowing cannot be used to meet your needs for food or shelter. Therefore, the payment for the lawn service is not in-kind income as defined in § 416.1102.
cases.situation: Leo receives SSI and lives alone in his own house. In June 2026 his brother pays a lawn service $120 to mow Leo's grass.
cases.question: Does the $120 count as income to Leo?
cases.ssa_answer: Not income: the mowing cannot be used to meet needs for food or shelter.

cases.title: A community buys a specially equipped van
cases.passage: Example 1: A community takes up a collection to buy you a specially equipped van, which is your only vehicle. The value of this gift is not income because the van does not provide you with food or shelter and will become an excluded nonliquid resource under § 416.1218 in the month following the month of receipt.
cases.situation: Sam receives SSI, lives alone and uses a wheelchair. In October 2026 his community takes up a collection and buys him a $38,000 specially equipped van, which is his only vehicle.
cases.question: Does the van count as income to Sam?
cases.ssa_answer: Not income: the van does not provide food or shelter and becomes an excluded resource the next month.

cases.title: A brother gives a new car
cases.passage: Stan Kowalski, an SSI recipient, receives a new car valued at $6,000 from their brother. Since a portion of the value of the car ($4,500) will become an excluded nonliquid resource in the next month, the value of the car is not income to Stan. NOTE: This example reflects the automobile resource exclusion policy in effect through March 2005 (See SI 01130.200C for the automobile exclusion policy beginning April 2005).
cases.situation: Stan receives SSI and lives alone. He does not own a car. In March 2026 his brother gives him a new car valued at $6,000.
cases.question: Does the car count as income to Stan?
cases.ssa_answer: Not income, because the car becomes an excluded resource the next month.

updated.note: SSA notes that this example reflects the car rule in effect through March 2005, when only part of the car's value was excluded. Since April 2005 one car is excluded whatever its value, so the answer is the same.

cases.title: Federal student aid, partly set aside
cases.passage: In September 2004, an SSI beneficiary receives $2,000 in grants and scholarships that are under Title IV of HEA. The SSI beneficiary uses $1,000 for tuition and fees and another $300 for books. The remaining $700 is set aside for unspecified reasons. The claims representative determines the $2,000 is excluded from income beginning September 2004 and the remaining $700 is excluded from resources. Educational assistance under Title IV of HEA or BIA is excluded from income and resources. Any interest or dividends earned on the $700 are also excluded from income.
cases.situation: Nina receives SSI, lives alone and attends college. In September 2026 she receives $2,000 in grants and scholarships under Title IV of the Higher Education Act. She uses $1,000 for tuition and fees and $300 for books, and sets the remaining $700 aside for no particular purpose.
cases.question: How much of the $2,000 counts as income to Nina in September 2026?
cases.ssa_answer: None. Educational assistance under Title IV of the Higher Education Act is excluded from income, and the $700 set aside is excluded from resources.

cases.title: A monthly "loan" with no duty to repay
cases.passage: EXAMPLE: An applicant applies for SSI in June 2011. They have no income and allege that their adult child provided them $200 cash per month as a loan. The applicant states that they would like to use their SSI benefits if approved to pay back the loan. When contacted, the adult child of the applicant states that although they would like the applicant to repay them, the applicant does not have to repay the loan. The CR determines that a bona fide loan does not exist because there is no obligation to repay.
cases.situation: Ray receives SSI, lives alone and has no other income. Every month in 2026 his adult child gives him $200 in cash and calls it a loan. Ray would like to repay it from his SSI, but his child says he does not have to. Consider July 2026.
cases.question: Does the $200 count as income to Ray in July 2026, and what is his SSI amount for that month?
cases.ssa_answer: There is no obligation to repay, so it is not a bona fide loan and the cash is income when received (SI 01120.220C.1.b). It comes every month, so the one-off exclusion does not apply; after the $20 general exclusion his SSI is $814.

cases.title: A plane ticket for a trip within the United States
cases.passage: The value of a ticket for domestic travel received by an individual, or their spouse, or parent whose income is subject to deeming is excluded from income if: • The ticket is received as a gift; and • The ticket is not converted to cash (e.g., cashed in, sold, etc.).
cases.situation: Ivy receives SSI and lives alone. In November 2026 her sister gives her a $420 round-trip plane ticket from Chicago to Phoenix to visit family. Ivy uses the ticket.
cases.question: Does the ticket count as income to Ivy?
cases.ssa_answer: Not income: a gift of a ticket for travel within the United States is excluded as long as it is not converted to cash.

cases.title: An aunt pays one electric bill
cases.passage: Generally, this exclusion applies to any type of unearned income. This exclusion also applies to in-kind support and maintenance (ISM) as described in SI 00835.000 and payments received for completing research surveys.
cases.situation: Rita receives SSI and lives alone with no other income. In May 2026 her aunt, who has not helped before and does not help again that year, pays Rita's $90 electric bill directly to the utility.
cases.question: How much in-kind support is charged in May 2026, and how much counts after the infrequent or irregular income exclusion?
cases.ssa_answer: In-kind support of $90. The infrequent or irregular income exclusion also applies to in-kind support, so $60 is excluded and $30 counts, before the $20 general exclusion.

cases.title: A father pays part of the rent each month
cases.passage: The PMV is the maximum amount of ISM that we can charge. We do not charge the PMV if an SSI claimant shows that: • the current market value (CMV) of any food, or shelter received, minus any payment the claimant makes for them, is less than the PMV; or • the actual amount someone else pays for the claimant's food or shelter is less than the PMV. The amount of ISM counted is the amount of the PMV described in SI 00835.300C.2. or the actual value, if the claimant rebuts the PMV and we establish a lower value. We explain the rebuttal rule procedures in SI 00835.320.
cases.situation: Omar receives SSI, lives alone in an apartment with $700 monthly rent and has no other income. Every month in 2026 his father pays $200 of the rent directly to the landlord and Omar pays the rest, and Omar shows SSA the receipts. Consider August 2026.
cases.question: How much in-kind support is charged in August 2026, and what is Omar's SSI amount for that month?
cases.ssa_answer: In-kind support of $200, the amount his father actually pays, because it is less than the cap. After the $20 general exclusion his SSI is $814.

cases.title: Cash from one aunt in March and again in April
cases.passage: Income is considered to be received infrequently if an individual receives it only once during a calendar quarter from a single source and the individual did not receive that type of income in the month immediately preceding that month or in the month immediately subsequent to that month, regardless of whether or not these payments occur in different calendar quarters.
cases.situation: Kim receives SSI and lives alone with no other income. Her aunt gives her $50 in cash on March 28, 2026 and another $50 in cash on April 3, 2026, and nothing else that year.
cases.question: How much of each $50 gift counts, after the infrequent or irregular income exclusion?
cases.ssa_answer: Neither gift is infrequent: the same aunt gave the same kind of income in the next month, even though it falls in another quarter. Both count in full.

cases.title: Birthday cash from two relatives in one month
cases.passage: Beginning September 8, 2006, infrequent income is defined as income that an individual receives only once during a calendar quarter from a single source, and which the individual did not receive in the month immediately preceding that month or in the month immediately subsequent to that month, regardless of whether or not those payments occur in different calendar quarters. We exclude the following amount of income which is received either infrequently or irregularly: • The first $30 per calendar quarter of earned income; and • The first $60 per calendar quarter of unearned income.
cases.situation: Lou receives SSI and lives alone with no other income. On his birthday, June 9, 2026, his uncle gives him $40 in cash and his godmother gives him $40 in cash. Neither gives him anything else that year.
cases.question: How much of the $80 counts, after the infrequent or irregular income exclusion?
cases.ssa_answer: Both gifts are infrequent, but the exclusion is the first $60 of unearned income in the quarter, not $60 per gift, so $20 counts.

cases.title: An uncle puts money in her ABLE account
cases.passage: Third party contributions: • are not income to the designated beneficiary; • are contributions made by persons other than the designated beneficiary; • are made with funds that do not otherwise belong, or are not otherwise due, to the designated beneficiary; • are made with the third party’s funds; and • are treated as a completed gift when made by a person other than the designated beneficiary NOTE: “Completed gift” refers to the IRS definition for gift-tax rules, not the definition of a gift in SI 00830.520. For ABLE, we exclude third party contributions, regardless of their status as a gift for SSI purposes.
cases.situation: Mae receives SSI, lives alone and has an ABLE account. In May 2026 her uncle deposits $500 of his own money into her ABLE account.
cases.question: Does the $500 count as income to Mae?
cases.ssa_answer: Not income: a contribution to her ABLE account made by someone else with their own money is not income to her.

cases.title: A son pays a dental insurance premium every month
cases.passage: Payment of an individual's bills (including supplementary medical insurance under title XVIII or other medical insurance premiums) by a third party directly to the supplier is not income. However, anything received in kind as a result of the payment is income if it is food or shelter.
cases.situation: Ben receives SSI and lives alone with no other income. Every month in 2026 his son pays Ben's $95 dental and vision insurance premium directly to the insurance company. Consider February 2026.
cases.question: Does the $95 count as income to Ben in February 2026?
cases.ssa_answer: Not income: medical insurance premiums paid by a third party directly to the insurer are not income.

cases.title: A sister pays the dentist
cases.passage: (a) Medical care and services. Medical care and services are not income if they are any of the following: (1) Given to you free of charge or paid for directly to the provider by someone else;
cases.situation: Ava receives SSI and lives alone. In July 2026 her sister pays a dentist $1,200 directly for Ava's crown.
cases.question: Does the $1,200 count as income to Ava?
cases.ssa_answer: Not income: medical care paid for directly to the provider by someone else is not income.

cases.title: A nephew pays for insulation and storm windows
cases.passage: (i) Weatherization assistance. Weatherization assistance (Examples: Insulation, storm doors and windows) is not income.
cases.situation: Hank receives SSI and lives alone in his own house. In October 2026 his nephew pays a contractor $1,800 to add attic insulation and install storm windows.
cases.question: Does the $1,800 count as income to Hank?
cases.ssa_answer: Not income: weatherization assistance, such as insulation and storm doors and windows, is not income.

cases.title: A son pays the whole rent every month
cases.passage: 2. Amount of PMV The amount of the PMV is equal to: a. Eligibility determinations One-third the Federal benefit rate (FBR) (in effect for the month in which ISM is received) for a claimant or an eligible couple, plus $20. b. Payment computations when ISM received in the budget month One-third the FBR (in effect for the month of payment computation) for an individual or an eligible couple, plus $20. Prior to January 01, 1995, we based the amount of the PMV used for payment computations on the amount of the FBR in effect for the budget month, rather than for the computation month. For a change in PMV computation policy effective January 1995, see SI 02005.001E.4. The PMV yields equal supplemental security insurance (SSI) payments for a claimant who is subject to the PMV, and a claimant who is subject to the VTR, if neither has other countable income.
cases.situation: Ellen receives SSI and lives alone in an apartment, with no other income. Every month in 2026 her son pays her $900 rent directly to the landlord. Consider October 2026.
cases.question: How much in-kind support is charged in October 2026, and what is Ellen's SSI amount for that month?
cases.ssa_answer: In-kind support capped at the presumed maximum value, one-third of the $994 federal rate plus $20, or $351.33. After the $20 general exclusion her SSI is $662.67, the same as under the one-third reduction.

cases.title: A sister pays next month's rent early
cases.passage: In-kind support and maintenance (ISM) from a TPVP is unearned income when an applicant or claimant first has use of the item. For more information on ISM, refer to SI 00835.310B. 1. Exception for TPVP as a gift ISM resulting from a TPVP is income in the month of the payment, rather than when an applicant or claimant first has use of the ISM, if: • the applicant or claimant obtains food or shelter using their own credit; and • a third party later makes a vendor payment for the items as a gift.
cases.situation: Jo receives SSI and lives alone in an apartment, with no other income. On March 25, 2026 her sister pays Jo's $300 April rent directly to the landlord, as a gift. Nobody else pays any of Jo's rent in 2026.
cases.question: How much in-kind support is charged in March and in April 2026?
cases.ssa_answer: In-kind support counts when she first has use of the shelter, which is April. The exception for a gift that pays for shelter she already obtained on her own credit does not apply, because April's rent was paid ahead.
cases.input_note: The payment is entered with the month it covers, April 2026.

cases.title: Her children give her a television
cases.passage: The value of any noncash item (other than an item of food or shelter) is not income if the item would become a partially or totally excluded nonliquid resource if retained into the month after the month of receipt.
cases.situation: Rosa receives SSI and lives alone. In December 2026 her children give her a $650 television for her living room.
cases.question: Does the television count as income to Rosa?
cases.ssa_answer: Not income: a television is a household good, which is excluded from resources whatever its value (SI 01130.430), and a non-cash item that would be an excluded resource is not income.

cases.title: A brother buys a power wheelchair
cases.passage: Items required because of an individual's physical or mental impairment, such as prosthetic devices or wheelchairs, are also personal effects.
cases.situation: Ted receives SSI and lives alone. In April 2026 his brother buys him a $4,500 power wheelchair.
cases.question: Does the wheelchair count as income to Ted?
cases.ssa_answer: Not income: a wheelchair is a personal effect, excluded from resources, and a non-cash gift that would be an excluded resource is not income (SI 00815.550).

cases.title: A grandmother buys clothes
cases.passage: NOTE: Clothing received before March 9, 2005 is counted as ISM. Clothing received on or after March 9, 2005 is not counted as ISM.
cases.situation: Lucy receives SSI and lives alone. In September 2026 her grandmother buys her $240 of clothes for the fall.
cases.question: Do the clothes count as income to Lucy?
cases.ssa_answer: Not income: clothing has not counted as in-kind support since March 9, 2005.

cases.title: Sunday dinners at a daughter's home
cases.passage: The individual receives ISM in the form of food outside a household setting such as a gift of meals at a relative's home.
cases.situation: Earl receives SSI and lives alone. Every Sunday in 2026 he eats dinner at his daughter's home, and she never asks him to pay. Consider November 2026, when the dinners are worth about $120.
cases.question: Do the dinners count as income to Earl in November 2026?
cases.ssa_answer: When written: in-kind support in the form of food. Since September 30, 2024: not income.

updated.note: SSA wrote this when food counted as in-kind support. A 2024 rule removed food from in-kind support, so since September 30, 2024 it is not income.

out_of_scope.what: A gift of a second car
out_of_scope.why: Giftwise does not ask whether the person already owns a car.

out_of_scope.what: A gift of the house she lives in
out_of_scope.why: Giftwise does not handle gifts of real property.

out_of_scope.what: Gift cards and gift certificates
out_of_scope.why: Giftwise has no gift-card route yet. SSA counts a card that can buy food or shelter, or can be resold, like cash.

out_of_scope.what: Housing help shared across a household or a couple
out_of_scope.why: Giftwise models one person living alone or in another person's household, not support split among several members.

out_of_scope.what: A co-owner paying mortgage arrears
out_of_scope.why: That payment is not a gift.

out_of_scope.what: Rent below market value from a parent or child
out_of_scope.why: Giftwise does not compute rental subsidies.

out_of_scope.what: Converting weekly or past-period bills to monthly amounts
out_of_scope.why: Giftwise takes monthly amounts as input.

out_of_scope.what: ABLE withdrawals and balances over $100,000
out_of_scope.why: These are about money leaving an ABLE account. Giftwise handles gifts going in.

out_of_scope.what: Deciding a living arrangement
out_of_scope.why: Giftwise takes the living arrangement as an input.

out_of_scope.what: A couple's wages, and rules from before July 2004
out_of_scope.why: Earned income for couples is not modeled, and the older rules no longer apply.

out_of_scope.what: A van given to a child's parents
out_of_scope.why: Deeming parents' income to a child is not modeled.

out_of_scope.what: A travel ticket cashed in, or a refundable ticket for travel abroad
out_of_scope.why: Giftwise does not ask whether a ticket can be refunded or where the trip goes.

out_of_scope.what: Loans from family that must be repaid
out_of_scope.why: A bona fide loan is not a gift, and Giftwise handles gifts.

out_of_scope.what: Help that a State certifies as home energy or support and maintenance assistance
out_of_scope.why: These are about charities and utilities certified by a State, not gifts from family.

out_of_scope.what: Cash from a private social services agency to pay a homemaker
out_of_scope.why: Giftwise handles gifts from people, not payments from programs.

out_of_scope.what: Support from households and institutions, wages from several jobs, and support from an absent parent
out_of_scope.why: Giftwise models gifts to one person, not household or institutional support, wages or child support.

out_of_scope.what: School money kept past nine months, spent on something else, or received under the rules before June 2004
out_of_scope.why: Giftwise does not follow how an education gift is spent in later months, and the older rules no longer apply.

out_of_scope.what: A child away at school whose parents' income is deemed
out_of_scope.why: Deeming parents' income to a child is not modeled.

out_of_scope.what: A gas bill for a home that also houses a business
out_of_scope.why: Giftwise does not split a bill between home and business use.

out_of_scope.what: The one-third reduction in a cost-of-living month
out_of_scope.why: Giftwise uses 2026 amounts only.
